As foreshadowed in the Introduction, a key finding from the cross-model comparison and the EZDM-DDM comparison in Tutorial 4 is that the hierarchical EZDM produces substantively identical conclusions to the DDM for drift-related research questions — at approximately 1,000× lower computational cost. This has practical implications that go beyond the staged workflow recommended above.

The original EZDM was designed as a quick approximation that sacrifices statistical sophistication for accessibility [@wagenmakers2007ezdiffusion]. Within `bmm`, however, the EZDM is no longer a standalone calculator but a full Bayesian hierarchical model: it estimates population-level effects with proper uncertainty quantification, supports arbitrary predictor structures via `bmf()`, and borrows strength across participants through hierarchical shrinkage. This addresses the two main criticisms of the original EZDM — sensitivity to contaminants (handled by the mixture preprocessing) and the absence of hierarchical structure [@ratcliff2008ez; @vanravenzwaaij2017ez]. Recent work formalizing the EZDM as a probabilistic proxy model [@chavez2025ez] provides theoretical justification for this approach, showing that the EZDM equations can serve as a likelihood function within a Bayesian generative framework.

For researchers whose primary interest is in how experimental manipulations affect drift — which is the most common use case for EAMs in cognitive psychology — the hierarchical EZDM in `bmm` may be sufficient as the primary analysis, not merely a screening step. Three conditions support this recommendation. First, the EZDM's statistical power for detecting condition effects on drift and bound is comparable to or higher than the full DDM's, because the simplifying assumptions reduce parameter uncertainty [@vanravenzwaaij2017ez]. Second, the hierarchical framework in `bmm` handles the sparse-cell problem that plagued the original EZDM — even the 4par model with four frequency levels and response coding converged cleanly despite cells with as few as three minority-boundary responses. Third, the computational savings (seconds vs. hours) make it practical to fit many candidate model specifications, conduct sensitivity analyses, and iterate on the predictor structure — activities that are prohibitively expensive with the DDM.

The EZDM is not appropriate when the research question specifically concerns the shape of the RT distribution (e.g., leading-edge effects, relative speed of errors vs. correct responses) or when precise estimates of bound or ndt are required. In these cases, the DDM remains the appropriate choice. The CSWALD occupies a useful middle ground — providing trial-level modeling at moderate computational cost — but its systematic bound underestimation limits its use for boundary-focused research questions.

## Limitations

Within the scope defined in the Introduction (simple DDM framework, two-choice tasks), several aspects were not demonstrated. We did not show between-trial variability parameters ($s_v$, $s_\zeta$, $s_\tau$), which can improve fit but create identifiability challenges [@luken2025identifiability; @boag2025expert]; researchers requiring the full seven-parameter DDM should consider alternatives such as HDDM [@wiecki2013hddm] or custom Stan implementations. We also did not cover formal model comparison techniques — bridge sampling and leave-one-out cross-validation are available via `brms` but were beyond the present scope.

## What to Do Next

Readers who have completed these tutorials are now equipped to apply EAMs to their own two-choice RT data. We recommend starting with the EZDM to explore condition effects, then fitting the CSWALD or DDM for confirmatory analysis — following the staged workflow described in the Practical Guidelines. The `bmm` package also supports mixture models for visual working memory [see @frischkorn2025tutorial for a companion tutorial] and continues to expand. For experimental design guidance, see @boag2025expert. Further resources include `bmm` documentation (<https://venpopov.github.io/bmm/>), `brms` documentation (<https://paul-buerkner.github.io/brms/>), @heathcote2015good on modeling best practices, and @mcelreath2020statistical on Bayesian data analysis. All data, code, and fitted models are available on OSF (<https://osf.io/XXXXX/>) and GitHub (<https://github.com/GidonFrischkorn/tutorial-eam-bmm>).

# References

# Appendix: Parameter Recovery on Simulated Data {.appendix}

To verify that the three `bmm` EAM implementations produce reliable estimates, we conducted a parameter recovery study using simulated data with known generating parameters. This complements the empirical tutorials and is consistent with the extensive parameter recovery literature for DDMs [@ratcliff2008diffusion; @vanravenzwaaij2017ez; @lerche2016model].^[The companion script `scripts/21_appendix_parameter_recovery.R` contains the full executable code.]

## Simulation Design

We generated data from a DDM with known parameters (drift: 2.5 for easy, 1.0 for hard; bound: 1.5; ndt: 0.3; $\zeta$: 0.5) for 50 participants, each completing 200 trials per condition. Individual-level parameters were drawn from normal distributions around the population means (see `scripts/20_prepare_simulated_data.R` for details). We then fitted the EZDM 3par, CSWALD crisk, and DDM to these data following the same `bmm` workflow used in the tutorials.

## Group-Level Recovery

```{r}
#| label: fig-recovery-group
#| fig-cap: "Group-level parameter recovery. Points indicate posterior means for each model; error bars show 95% credible intervals. Dashed lines mark the true generating values. All three models recover drift and ndt accurately. The CSWALD crisk shows the expected ~10% underestimation of bound."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "21_recovery_group.pdf"))
```

All three models recovered the generating parameters within their 95% credible intervals (@fig-recovery-group). Drift and ndt estimates were highly consistent across models. The CSWALD crisk showed the expected ~10% underestimation of bound, consistent with the competing-risks approximation documented in the main tutorials.

## Subject-Level Recovery

Beyond group-level means, we evaluated whether the models recover individual differences by correlating true participant-level parameters with their posterior estimates.

```{r}
#| label: fig-recovery-subject
#| fig-cap: "Subject-level parameter recovery. Each point represents one participant; the x-axis shows the true generating value and the y-axis the recovered posterior mean. High correlations indicate that the models preserve the rank ordering of individual differences. Panels show drift (easy condition), bound, and ndt across all three models."
#| eval: true
#| echo: false
knitr::include_graphics(here("figures", "21_recovery_subject.pdf"))
```

Subject-level correlations between true and recovered parameters were high across all models (@fig-recovery-subject), ranging from $r$ = `r recovery_r_min` to `r recovery_r_max` (median $r$ = `r recovery_r_median`). These strong correlations indicate that the hierarchical structure in `bmm` preserves individual differences while borrowing strength across participants — an essential property for studies that use EAM parameters as individual difference measures. The results are consistent with published recovery studies and confirm that all three `bmm` implementations produce reliable estimates at both the group and individual level under controlled conditions.
